rows: The three pairs of side eyes together cover almost the whole circle round the spider, about 360 degrees, with a small overlap in front. Their sharpness is modest. The best measured, in Evarcha, is 1.3 cycles per degree, and other species fall as low as 0.3, so the wide picture is soft.

Two large forward-facing eyes give the sharp picture, and each looks at a field only about 5 degrees wide. A typical species such as Phidippus johnsoni resolves about 3.8 cycles per degree. Portia reaches 12.5, an exceptional figure for a spider.
Only movement reaches the side eyes

The side eyes behave as though completely blind to stationary things. A target already in view starts a turn only when it moves, and a light that only switches on and off starts none. A target has to be wider than about 0.7 degrees and move about 1 degree to be seen.

The side eyes of the species tested hold a single type of receptor, peaking near 535 nm, so they cannot tell colours apart. The principal eyes of most jumping spiders hold two types, an ultraviolet one near 370 nm and a green one near 530 nm. Colour therefore reaches the small sharp spot and the wide picture stays grey. A few species, such as Habronattus, add a third type in the centre of the retina, and this view draws the common two.

The principal eyes have retinas that move behind fixed lenses. They sweep side to side across what they inspect, with a period of 1 to 2 seconds and an amplitude of at least 2 degrees. A large shift of 15 degrees completes within a tenth of a second.
Jumping spiders freeze at low airborne tones near 80 Hz, which their leg hairs pick up, and courting males send vibrations through the ground. This picture leaves both out.

The grey of the wide picture is the app's own choice, drawn from the finding of a single receptor type in the side eyes. The movement gate and the sweep of the sharp spot are the app's own settings, shaped by what the records describe about movement and scanning. The sharp spot is drawn as an ellipse, with a colour matrix standing in for the two pigments. The whole-picture sharpness and the sharpness of the spot apply figures from single species or a worked conversion to the whole family. The drawing options are the app's own.

claims.how: The record states a 360 degree field of view for the four pairs of eyes combined.
The record gives 1.3 cycles per degree for the antero-lateral eyes of Evarcha blancardi, used here for the whole wide picture.
Visual angle of 0.13 degrees gives 1/(2 x 0.13) = 3.85, which the record gives as 3.8 cycles per degree.
The record gives a visual field of around 5 degrees for each principal eye.
Peaks of 370 nm (UV cells in Phidippus regius) and 530 nm (green class in Habronattus pyrrithrix) are taken directly from the two records.

quotes.quote: Combined, the four pairs of eyes give the spider a 360° field of view.
to 1.3 cycles/degree, as in Evarcha blancardi
with a small visual field of around 5 deg each
